In [[metric geometry]], a '''geodesic bicombing''' distinguishes a class of [[Geodesic|geodesics]] of a [[metric space]]. The study of metric spaces with distinguished geodesics traces back to the work of the mathematician [[Herbert Busemann]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Busemann, Herbert (1905-)|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/908865701|title=Spaces with distinguished geodesics|date=1987|publisher=Dekker|isbn=0-8247-7545-7|oclc=908865701}}</ref> The convention to call a collection of paths of a metric space bicombing is due to [[William Thurston]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Epstein, D. B. A.|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/911329802|title=Word processing in groups|date=1992|publisher=Jones and Bartlett Publishers|isbn=0-86720-244-0|pages=84|oclc=911329802}}</ref> By imposing a weak global [[non-positive curvature]] condition on a geodesic bicombing several results from the theory of [[CAT(k) space|CAT(0) spaces]] and [[Banach space]] theory may be recovered in a more general setting. 

== Definition ==
Let <math>(X,d)</math> be a metric space. A map <math>\sigma\colon X\times X\times [0,1]\to X</math> is a ''geodesic bicombing'' if for all points <math>x,y\in X</math> the map <math>\sigma_{xy}(\cdot):=\sigma(x,y,\cdot)</math> is a unit speed metric geodesic from <math>x</math> to <math>y</math>, that is, <math>\sigma_{xy}(0)=x</math>, <math>\sigma_{xy}(1)=y</math> and <math>d(\sigma_{xy}(s), \sigma_{xy}(t))=\vert s-t\vert d(x,y)</math> for all real numbers <math>s,t\in [0,1]</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Descombes|first1=Dominic|last2=Lang|first2=Urs|date=2015|title=Convex geodesic bicombings and hyperbolicity|journal=[[Geometriae Dedicata]]|language=en|volume=177|issue=1|pages=367–384|doi=10.1007/s10711-014-9994-y|doi-access=free|issn=0046-5755|hdl=20.500.11850/87627|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

== Different classes of geodesic bicombings ==
A geodesic bicombing <math>\sigma\colon X\times X\times [0,1]\to X</math> is:

* ''reversible'' if <math display="block">\sigma_{xy}(t)=\sigma_{yx}(1-t)</math> for all <math>x,y\in X</math> and <math>t\in [0,1]</math>.
* ''consistent'' if <math display="block">\sigma_{xy}((1-\lambda)s+\lambda t)=\sigma_{pq}(\lambda)</math> whenever <math>x,y\in X, 0\leq s\leq t\leq 1, p:=\sigma_{xy}(s), q:=\sigma_{xy}(t), </math>and <math>\lambda\in [0,1]</math>.

*''conical'' if <math display="block">d(\sigma_{xy}(t), \sigma_{x^\prime y^\prime}(t))\leq (1-t)d(x,x^\prime)+t d(y,y^\prime)</math> for all <math>x,x^\prime, y, y^\prime\in X</math> and <math>t\in [0,1]</math>.
*''convex'' if  <math display="block">t\mapsto d(\sigma_{xy}(t), \sigma_{x^\prime y^\prime}(t)) </math> is a convex function on <math>[0,1]</math> for all <math>x,x^\prime, y, y^\prime\in X</math>.

== Examples ==
Examples of metric spaces with a conical geodesic bicombing include:

* Banach spaces.
* CAT(0) spaces.
* [[Injective metric space|injective metric spaces]].
*the spaces <math>(P_1(X),W_1),</math> where <math>W_1</math> is the first [[Wasserstein distance]].
* any [[ultralimit]] or 1-Lipschitz [[Retraction (category theory)|retraction]] of the above.

== Properties ==

*Every consistent conical geodesic bicombing is convex.
*Every convex geodesic bicombing is conical, but the reverse implication does not hold in general. 
* Every [[proper metric space]] with a conical geodesic bicombing admits a convex geodesic bicombing.<ref name=":0" />
* Every [[complete metric space]] with a conical geodesic bicombing admits a reversible conical geodesic bicombing.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Basso|first1=Giuliano|last2=Miesch|first2=Benjamin|date=2019|title=Conical geodesic bicombings on subsets of normed vector spaces|url=https://www.degruyter.com/view/j/advgeom.2019.19.issue-2/advgeom-2018-0008/advgeom-2018-0008.xml|journal=[[Advances in Geometry]]|volume=19|issue=2|pages=151–164|doi=10.1515/advgeom-2018-0008|issn=1615-7168|arxiv=1604.04163|hdl=20.500.11850/340286 |s2cid=15595365 }}</ref>
